clue.text: "We turn for a short time from the topics of the day to commemorate, in all love and reverence, the genius and virtues of John Milton, the 12, the 10, the 14, the g24 of ___ 11, the 16 and the 19 of ___ 28" (Macaulay, making the most of his length)

definitions.text: "We turn for a short time from the topics of the day to commemorate, in all love and reverence, the genius and virtues of John Milton, the 12, the 10, the 14, the g24 of ___ 11, the 16 and the 19 of ___ 28" (Macaulay, making the most of his length)

parts.words: "We turn for a short time from the topics of the day to commemorate, in all love and reverence, the genius and virtues of John Milton, the 12, the 10, the 14, the g24 of ___ 11, the 16 and the 19 of ___ 28" (Macaulay, making the most of his length)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank: Macaulay's tribute to Milton uses the same national adjective in both gaps, before literature and before liberty, and the seven-letter word is made the most of by appearing twice

explanation.surface: A quotation from Macaulay's essay on Milton, with the gaps for the solver to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The numbers inside the quotation are other answers: POET, STATESMAN, PHILOSOPHER, GLORY (G plus the 24-down parrot), LITERATURE, CHAMPION, MARTYR and LIBERTY. The puzzle marks 400 years since Milton's birth in 1608.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaulay's line praises Milton as the glory of the nation's literature and the martyr of the nation's liberty, so the missing adjective is the national one.

clue.text: Forties cry that's on the up when winning first gold

indicators.note: the answer gains extra letters to make the cry, so going back the other way they are removed

parts.note: Excelsior, Latin for 'higher', is a cry of aspiration, made famous by Longfellow's poem
I is the Roman numeral one, the first
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A wartime cry from the 1940s that rises when gold is won first.
explanation.walkthrough: XL is Roman 40, so forties are XLs, said 'ex-els'. Winning I and OR turns the answer into the upward cry Excelsior.
explanation.definitionFit: XL is the Roman numeral for forty, so several forties are XLs, pronounced as the answer.

clue.text: Had no choice with river entering cave

indicators.note: the river letter enters, going inside the other piece

parts.note: 'got to' means had to, had no choice

explanation.surface: Someone forced to go into a cave as a river flows in.
explanation.definitionFit: A grotto is a small picturesque cave.

clue.text: The unconscious revelation of how fast the Queen goes after a pub

indicators.note: the Queen's pace goes after the pub, so it follows it

parts.note: an inn is a pub
ER is the Queen, Elizabeth Regina, and ER'S is the Queen's
pace is speed, how fast one goes

explanation.surface: A dream revelation about how quickly the monarch walks once she leaves the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The unconscious' looks like a noun for a sleeper; it is the mind's hidden depths. ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Inner space is a term for the unconscious mind, the realm within as opposed to outer space.

clue.text: Holds view that prevails

definitions.meaning: as in 'legend ... that', to have it is to hold or maintain a view
in a vote 'the ayes have it': the side that wins is said to have it

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both maintains or asserts and, in a vote, wins the day, as in 'the ayes have it'.

clue.text: Shocking omission of "the plural of mou__e"

parts.note: complete the grammar rule about one small rodent and many, write it without spaces, and the run sitting in the gap is the word left out

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson with a word missing is presented as something scandalous.
explanation.walkthrough: Write 'mouse is mice' without spaces: between MOU and the closing E sit the letters SE IS MIC, which is the omitted run.
explanation.definitionFit: Seismic means relating to earthquakes, and figuratively shocking or of enormous impact.

clue.text: At first, ducks are playing in the well

indicators.note: playing about, the letters are rearranged

parts.note: a duck is a zero score in cricket, the letter O, and two make OO

explanation.surface: Ducks splashing about at the start in a well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' looks like a first-letter instruction; it is anagram fodder. 'are' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A stairwell's bottom is the foot of the stairs, so the well is where the stairfoot lies.

clue.text: I'm unknown, as they say: I have a high life

parts.note: in country dialect 'I be' stands for I am
X is the algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: Someone describing their mystery status and lofty existence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as they say' flags the dialect form I BE for I'm, not a sound-alike. The definition speaks as the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibex is a wild mountain goat living on high Alpine crags, so it has a high life.

clue.text: Big beasts dropping a subject with rounds in it

indicators.note: the rounds go inside the shortened subject
the letter a is let fall out of the subject

parts.note: maths is a school subject
ammunition comes in rounds; ammo is the short form

explanation.surface: Large animals losing a topic with bullets inside it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with rounds in it' reads as the subject's description; 'in it' is the container signal, after A is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Mammoths were huge extinct elephants, and the word also means anything enormous.

clue.text: Generalissimo with true twist of belt

parts.note: a generalissimo is a commander-in-chief, abbreviated C-in-C

indicators.note: giving a twist to the word rearranges its letters

explanation.surface: A supreme commander with a genuine twist on his belt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twist of' rearranges the four letters of 'true'; 'with' joins them to the military abbreviation C-in-C.
explanation.definitionFit: A cincture is a girdle or belt, especially one worn with a vestment.

clue.text: Bird on pole, no friend to our friend

parts.note: a crow is a common black bird
N is the north pole

explanation.surface: A bird perched on a pole is said to be unfriendly to someone we like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our friend' is Milton, the puzzle's subject, a republican who defended the execution of Charles I.
explanation.definitionFit: The monarchy, which Milton the republican opposed, was hardly a friend to the poet being celebrated.

clue.text: Periodically new American island

parts.note: the States is the everyday name for the USA
the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: An American island that keeps being renewed every so often.
explanation.walkthrough: The New Statesman is a British weekly magazine, so the word made 'new' is a periodical; the quotation in 1-across also defines it.
explanation.definitionFit: Prefixed by New, the word names a long-running British political weekly, a periodical.

clue.text: In a trap? Repeat all but the last letters

indicators.note: the remaining letters of the repeat word go inside the trap word

parts.note: a lure is a decoy or trap

indicators.note: the final letter of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: to iterate is to repeat

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about being trapped followed by an instruction to repeat everything but the final letters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters' looks like part of the instruction; it is the definition, in the sense of 'a man of letters'.
explanation.definitionFit: Letters is the old collective word for written works and learning, as in 'man of letters'.

clue.text: Cocktail of drugs for liner

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the drug names are mixed up

parts.note: pot is a slang name for cannabis
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A mixture of drugs is offered as something for an ocean liner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liner' looks like a ship; it is someone who writes lines.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of verse produces lines, so a liner in the cryptic sense is a poet.

clue.text: Balcony spattered with mud, but they are far from wet …

indicators.note: spattering scatters things, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

explanation.surface: A balcony splashed with mud, though the people on it are bone dry.
explanation.walkthrough: In British politics 'wets' were moderate Tories under Thatcher; the Monday Club is a hard-right Conservative group, far from wet. 'with' links the fodder BALCONY and MUD.
explanation.definitionFit: The Monday Club is a right-wing Conservative pressure group, the opposite of the moderate wets.

clue.text: 23 with a stone?

parts.note: 23 is the German dialectician, a thinker by trade; add a stone and you get the alchemists' legendary stone that turns base metal into gold

explanation.surface: A cross-reference asks what 23 would be if given a stone.
explanation.walkthrough: The philosopher's stone was the alchemists' goal; Hegel, the 23-down answer, is a member of the profession.
explanation.definitionFit: Hegel was a thinker of the profession named, and with a stone the word gives the alchemists' philosopher's stone.

clue.text: … far from that kind of Tory, holding Ulster in an exhausted state

indicators.note: the Tory phrase holds the Ulster letters inside it

parts.note: a One Nation Tory, from Disraeli's ideal, is a moderate; one becomes I, giving I NATION
NI is Northern Ireland, often called Ulster

explanation.surface: Continuing 13: hard-liners are far from moderate Tories, and keeping Ulster leaves them worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues 13-down: the Monday Club is far from One Nation Tories (moderate Conservatives). 'far from' and 'in' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Inanition is exhaustion caused by lack of nourishment, an exhausted state.

clue.text: Jolly good Tory eating meat? Good!

indicators.note: the Tory word eats the other pieces, which go inside it

parts.note: CON is short for Conservative
ham is a meat
pi, short for pious, means good

explanation.surface: A cheery Tory tucking into meat and pronouncing it good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champion!' is northern English slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Champion as an exclamation is dated British slang meaning excellent, like jolly good.

clue.text: Commit patricide by one with binding attachment

parts.note: to kill one's father is to end one's pa
per means for each, by one

explanation.surface: A murderous instruction to kill one's father, paired with something attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An endpaper is the sheet pasted to the inside of a book's cover, attached to the binding.

clue.text: Fancy end with hard fact, not out of factory

indicators.note: fancy as a verb means imagine, and here it signals the letters are rearranged into a new design

explanation.surface: A fancy ending made of hard fact, not mass-produced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' links the three fodder words END, HARD and FACT, whose eleven letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Something handcrafted is made by hand, rather than manufactured in a factory.

clue.text: Ross's leader following his follower, mostly one that suffers

indicators.note: the Ross letter comes after the rest
only the greater part of the follower word is used, the start falling away

parts.note: the old Scottish county was Ross and Cromarty, so Cromarty follows Ross

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Ross's leader trails behind his loyal follower, who mostly suffers.
explanation.walkthrough: Ross and Cromarty was a Scottish county, so Cromarty is Ross's follower; 'mostly' loses its first three letters, and 'following' puts Ross's leader after.
explanation.definitionFit: A martyr suffers or dies for a cause, one who endures great suffering.

clue.text: Large fish for this bird?

parts.note: OS is outsize, a large clothing size
a fish-eating raptor hunts fish as its prey

explanation.surface: A question about how big a fish this bird catches.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the answer: the bird takes large fish, which are its prey.
explanation.definitionFit: The osprey is a raptor that dives for fish, so large fish are its food.

clue.text: Be depressed about arrangement of 12's work

indicators.note: an arrangement reorders things, so the letters of the work are rearranged

parts.note: 12-across is a writer of verse, whose work is a poem

explanation.surface: Feeling low about how a poet's work has been set out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is a link word, not a reversal; the four letters of the 12-across's work are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: To mope is to sulk listlessly, feeling sorry for oneself.

clue.text: A very long way to the galaxy's boundaries, tossed around among storytellers

indicators.note: the scrambled letters sit within the storytellers word

parts.note: liars tell stories, i.e. untruths

indicators.note: tossing things around jumbles them, so the letters are mixed
the boundaries of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Measuring a vast distance to the edge of the galaxy, flung about among fabulists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tossed around' scrambles 'the' with the galaxy's first and last letters, and 'among' sets that inside the storytellers.
explanation.definitionFit: A light year is the distance light travels in a year, so the plural is an immense distance.

clue.text: Dialectician providing hair fixer for men?

parts.note: he, as in he-goat, marks the male
gel is used to fix hair

explanation.surface: Some product or other offers hair gel for men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'providing' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Georg Hegel, the German philosopher, is famous for his dialectic of thesis, antithesis and synthesis.

clue.text: Parrot on top of one of the Roses?

annotationWithheld.why: Parrot on top of one of the Roses? (LORY): 'Parrot' defines it, but 'on top of one of the Roses?' gives no letters I can derive or source (perhaps a rose called Glory, G on top of it), so the wordplay is unparsed
annotationWithheld.clue: Parrot on top of one of the Roses?

clue.text: Monkey moving about on the up

parts.note: monkey is a playful name for a mischievous child, an imp
roving means wandering about

explanation.surface: A monkey travelling around on its way upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting better means improving, like a business that is on the up.

clue.text: The land across the sea shows when to see you

indicators.note: shows as in 'presents itself as': the French phrase, spoken, comes across as an English word

parts.note: across the Channel, in French, the land is la terre

explanation.surface: Somewhere overseas reveals the time of the next meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: The French 'la terre' said in an English mouth is close to the casual farewell's key word.
explanation.definitionFit: 'See you later' is a farewell, so the word tells when the next meeting will be.

clue.text: Indian writer's granny's eaten a fish

indicators.note: the granny word has eaten the other pieces, which go inside it

parts.note: nan is a British familiar word for grandmother; the 's stands for has
a ray is a flat sea fish

explanation.surface: An Indian author's grandmother has swallowed a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: R. K. Narayan wrote the Malgudi novels. The 's of granny's reads as 'has', so granny has eaten A RAY.
explanation.definitionFit: R. K. Narayan was a celebrated Indian novelist writing in English.

clue.text: Department store wrecked by half 11

indicators.note: something wrecked is broken up, so the letters are reassembled
half of the 11-across answer, its first five letters

explanation.surface: A shop ruined by half of eleven o'clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes the first five letters of 11-across, LITER, and 'wrecked' rearranges BY plus LITER. Liberty is a famous London department store.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberty is a long-established department store on Regent Street in London.
